title: Betye Saar, Picasso, BlackStar

body:
Weekly Newsletter
                The little-known story of a stolen Picasso that once belonged to the Guggenheim Museum, Zeitz MOCAA’s new leader, and the discovery of a 2,000-year-old Roman shipwreck. 
            
                
                                
                            
                
            
        
            Summer and the streets are teeming with beautiful young people. In a shop window, I catch my reflection staring at me with contempt. I need a haircut but have no barber to go to. The last one talked too much about his prostate and made me look like the reincarnation of Saddam Hussein. I spot a pretty well-known artist walking towards me. We’ve met and emailed before, but we can’t really be called friends. We exchange side glances and notice each other, but make an unspoken agreement to keep walking anyway. In hindsight, I should've stopped to say hi. But it was a muggy day and it was hard enough to just exist. I put on my dark Ray-Bans to avoid any more awkward encounters. Speaking of Ray-Bans, you should read the piece on the recent guerrilla action by the group Everyone Hates Elon. It’s a poster of Jeffrey Epstein wearing Meta’s camera glasses, captioned: “Glasses for people who don’t do consent.”Driving across Brooklyn, blasting Pink Floyd, I hit the brakes when a flock of geese starts waddling across the bridge over Newtown Creek. They seem to enjoy the attention from charmed drivers filming on their phones. They don't know about the huge poultry slaughterhouse on the other side.  Neighborhoods around me change from White to Hasidic to Black and Brown. Someone on the radio says the president has completely lost his mind. An expert explains that it takes 17 generations to overcome a major generational trauma. Sorry, mister, but I don’t think I can wait that long. —Hakim Bishara, editor-in-chief 

	
		
			How Betye Saar Came to Be
		
	
	
		There is an African Adinkra symbol, “Sankofa,” that means “go back and get it.” It’s intended to preach the importance of looking to the past when shaping the future, and to share wisdom between generations. On the occasion of her 100th birthday, Roberts Projects in Los Angeles organized an exhibition to recognize the earliest professional works of Betye Saar — the prolific assemblage artist who prodded the psyche of the Black American experience for over seven decades before her death last month. The show sheds light on a lesser-known facet of her canon: costume design. 
      
Through the over 200 archival objects in the show, one gets a good sense of the multiple pots Saar had her fingers in at the beginning of her career. Costume design, dancing (a full-wall photo of a young dancing Saar acts as the exhibition greeter), photography, drawing, jewelry, garments, greeting cards, album covers, and more are on view. The range depicts Saar’s broad curiosities, but it also underlines her particular skill in identifying various potentials and fitting them together. 
	
	
		Read More
	

NewsThe Joan Mitchell Foundation announces the recipients of its 2026 Fellowships, one of the most coveted prizes awarded to visual artists in the United States. Russian missile attacks have damaged or destroyed over 4,500 cultural sites, according to a statement from Ukraine’s Ministry of Culture.A new mock ad by the activism group Everyone Hates Elon depicts the Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses on a photo of Jeffrey Epstein, overlaid with the statement, “Glasses for people who don’t do consent.”A Picasso that vanished from the University of Pittsburgh in 1961 has resurfaced — and the Guggenheim is headed to court to get it back.Elvira Dyangani Ose will succeed Koyo Kouoh as the artistic director of Zeitz Museum of Contemporary Art Africa in Cape Town, South Africa.The National Gallery of Art is studying the possible impact of racecar vibrations on artwork ahead of Trump’s “Freedom 250 Grand Prix.”A 2,300-year-old papyrus fragment containing parts of Homer’s Odyssey is now on view at the Metropolitan Museum of Art.A 17th-century still life that had gathered dust for decades in storage at the National Museum of Norway is set to resurface in a forthcoming exhibition, where it will be publicly attributed to the Flemish painter Clara Peeters for the first time.While exploring the warm waters of the Sicilian coast last week, two Italian divers discovered hundreds of clay vessels piled atop an approximately 2,000-year-old Roman shipwreck.The San Diego Museum of Art lays off 11 employees, citing “rising operational costs” and funding uncertainties.“The Bowery: Devil’s Mile,” opening September 24 at the New Museum, traces 400 years of the iconic strip known as a destination for fun, however raucous or refined.From Our Critics

			10 Photo Books to Read This Month
		
	
	
		Hal Fischer’s archive of queer fashion, Sophie Rivera’s portraits of Nuyorican communities, Rania Matar’s love letter to Lebanon, and more new titles to check out from photo book publishers. 
	
	
		Read More
	

In Memoriam: This week, we honor Christian Bernard, the founding museum director; Albert “Al” Gury, an artist who shaped PAFA; Hermione Carline, a painter of transience, and others. A View From the Easel: Lilit Martirosyan summons the memories embedded in wool and soil while the sounds of opera arias fill her studio.Required Reading: Nancy Spero’s pro-choice art, Valentina Di Liscia on “Casa Cueva,” Brooklyn’s smallest museum, Jamaica Kincaid’s eyebrows, Israeli cuisine and Palestinian erasure, and more.

title: Mary Heilmann, Influential Abstract Painter, Dead at 86
description: Mary Heilmann, an influential abstract painter who received her first solo exhibition in a New York museum in her 60s, died at 86 on Friday in River
body:
Mary Heilmann, an influential abstract painter who received her first solo exhibition in a New York museum in her 60s, died at 86 on Friday in Riverhead, New York. Her studio announced the news in an Instagram posting, adding that she died “due to complications from a fall.”

	Heilmann was a pioneering abstract painter who blended elements from pop culture, craft, and art history with ease and wit. In the catalog for Heilmann’s 2008 retrospective at the New Museum—also her first solo at a New York institution—art critic Dave Hickey wrote, “The canons of geometric abstraction, Color Field painting, and Minimalism are honored in the spirit but not in the letter. In Heilmann’s synthesis, they are straightforwardly looted as available precedents.”
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	That exhibition had already appeared at the Orange County Museum of Art in Newport Beach, California and the Contemporary Art Museum Houston and received much acclaim. Prior to that show, she had received a survey at the ICA Boston in 1990 and the exhibition “All Tomorrows Parties” at the Vienna Secession in Austria. She had also exhibited in the 1972, 1989, and 2008 editions of the Whitney Biennial.

	The New Museum show, however, gained her widespread attention and accolades, leading to a steady parade of exhibitions at institutions like the Whitney, the Bonnefantenmuseum in the Netherlands, the Hamburger Bahnhof in Berlin, Whitechapel Gallery in London, Dia Beacon, and the Whitney (again), which closed in January.

	Heilmann has been credited as a major influence on a generation of painters, with Ellsworth Kelly going so far as to say, on the occasion of the 2008 show, that she was “the best of the new abstractionists.” She was also a longtime artist of Hauser & Wirth, having done her first show with the gallery in 1997, just five years after the gallery was founded.

	“Manuela, Ursula and I met Mary in the spring of 1994. We were introduced to her by the artist Patty Martori and we started to collect her work right away,” Iwan Wirth, president of Hauser & Wirth, reflected in a statement. “Mary also introduced us to other artists she knew and admired like Louise Bourgeois. Our first project with Mary was her book The All Night Movie, which is kind of an autobiography as an artist book, and our first show with her came along in 1997, with so many to follow. Mary was really our first love.”
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Mary Heilmann in her studio on Hyde Street, San Francisco CA, ca. 1979
									Photo Mark Magill/Courtesy the artist, Hauser & Wirth and 303 Gallery, New York
	



	Mary Ann Heilmann was born in San Francisco on January 3, 1940. Born to Mary Florence Webb, a nurse, and John Sherman Heilmann, a civil engineer, Heilmann split her childhood between the Bay Area and, after her father took a job building freeways, Los Angeles, by way of El Segundo, a seaside village nearby. 

	Early on, Heilmann was exposed to the free speech movement, the Beat Generation, and surf culture, all of which made a strong impression on the young artist. She started as a ceramicist, earning her bachelor’s from the University of California, Santa Barbara in 1962. She later enrolled at UC Berkeley so that she could study ceramics under Peter Voulkos, who applied Abstract Expressionist ideas to the medium.

	After completing her MFA at Berkeley in 1967, Heilmann moved to New York where she began painting, favoring bright acrylic paints and lush color palettes, referring to the works as “sculptural material.” She often blurred the boundary between her artworks and the exhibition space.

	She first gained recognition when she was included in the 1972 Whitney Annual Exhibition, the precursor to the Biennial.

	“In what she considered one of the most important technical breakthroughs of her career,” Hauser & Wirth has written about that period of Heilmann’s career, “she experimented with layering controverting painting techniques: a foundational layer, often a gestural composition, covered in parts with masking tape and overpainted with a second layer, often a hard-edge composition. The result, formally and technically original, exemplifies the rapturous freedom that would come to define Heilmann’s oeuvre.”
	


			
			
			
	
			
					Mary Heilmann, Surfing on Acid, 2005.
	



	As her work developed in the ’70s and ’80s, Heilmann began transforming personal references like music, waves, California highways, and other symbols into more simple visual forms like circles, squares, and stripes. Works were often titled after a popular song or an experience like Driving at Night in an effort to connect with the audience. Throughout the ’90s and aughts, she moved closer to the center of the art world as her work gained recognition, as well a fellowship from the Anonymous Was a Woman Foundation and grants from the National Endowment for the Arts and the Guggenheim Foundation. For decades, Heilmann supported her practice as a professor, first at Stony Brook University and later at the School of Visual Arts in New York.

	In her twilight years, she lived in Bridgehampton, New York, after visiting the area regularly since the 1960s. Heilmann, who never married or had children, is survived by her nieces, Ann Jaime and Chris Heilmann, her nephew, John Heilmann, Jr., and their families.

title: Why Brancusi’s Sleek, Streamlined Sculptures Still Seduce
description:
“The legendary actress visits Christie’s galleries at Rockefeller Center and finds herself captivated by the gilded sculpture.” 

	Thus trumpets the
body:
“The legendary actress visits Christie’s galleries at Rockefeller Center and finds herself captivated by the gilded sculpture.” 

	Thus trumpets the tagline for Nicole Kidman’s assignation with Constantin Brancusi’s bronze and gold leaf Danaïde (1913), circulated online this past spring in advance of the work’s auction.  The “cinematic short film” produced by Christie’s indeed reveals the Hollywood star finding herself… duly captivated.

	She rushes an unnamed caller off the phone to stalk the sculpture in her stilettos from behind a circular curtain. To the tune of David Bowie’s “Golden Years,” Kidman gazes fixedly into Danaïde’s burnished, nearly vacant visage. The camera cuts intermittently to a speculative montage of her inner experience. 
	

	
		Related Articles
	


	Like some ancient oracle, the sculpture’s mere presence unleashes a series of visionary insights into its presumed (read: decidedly fantastical) origins: from all manner of Greek statuary to eastern Buddhas, from the latter-day pre-Raphaelite painting The Danaïdes (1904) by John William Waterhouse to (utterly anachronistically) Alberto Giacometti’s 1951 sculpture The Chariot (Does Christie’s not employ a single art historian among its marketing ranks?). 

	Stare into the abyss and the abyss stares back. Or so Kidman’s filmed epiphany would suggest. She ends up dancing around the sculpture with tousled hair like some latter-day, midtown Maenad, her face—and ostensibly her soul—convulsed by the sculpture’s extrasensory revelations. 

	Danaïde left the block for a record $107.6 million, breaking the record for the auctioned sale of a sculpture. Whether Kidman’s performance inched the price upward remains unclear. It nevertheless undeniably played into a moment of renewed attention to the artist.


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin. 
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	BEFORE HIS DEATH in Paris at the age of 81, the Romanian-born Brancusi (1876–1957) bequeathed his estate to the French government on one condition: that his 15th arrondissement studio be reconstructed and preserved in perpetuity. Ongoing renovations of the Centre Pompidou, which has long since hosted the “Atelier Brancusi” in its abutting plaza, have set the workspace and its wide-ranging contents on the road. 
	

	They landed this summer at Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie, the first major exhibition of Brancusi’s work in Germany for a half century. MoMA will mount its own version of the show in October. More than 150 sculptures—along with works on paper, photographs, and extensive archival material—provide the occasion for an expansive survey of one of the twentieth century’s most influential artists. The host institutions have been given free curatorial rein. 


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin.
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	Designed by Mies van der Rohe, Berlin’s Neue Nationalgalerie offers up the ideal venue for Brancusi’s crisp distillations of form, at least in theory. Interrupted by just four load-bearing columns in its main gallery space, the open plan practically begs for vertical interventions by Brancusi—one of the twentieth-century artists most in tune with van der Rohe’s consummately modernist, “Less is More” sobriety. 

	In practice, puzzling choices by curators Klaus Biesenbach and Maike Steinkamp rendered the experiment fraught in places. Conservation questions surely informed certain placements (glass vitrines, elevated platforms). Yet the setting of so many of the sculptures against the wall impeded the kind of looking the works demand. Bird in Space (1923) was made to look decidedly agoraphobic. One had to crane one’s neck (almost impossibly) to get a glimpse of the maquette which Brancusi made for the lintel of the Kiss gate (1935–37)—part of his war memorial in Târgu Jiu, Romania. 
	


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin.
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	The exhibition did lend welcome attention to the full gamut of Brancusi’s media and formats.  Present in photographic form, his 1918 Endless Column (part of the same Târgu Jiu complex) forms just one of several arresting architectural designs. These also offer oblique insight into the relation of his sculptures to their carved bases, miniature structures in their own right, after all, which often rival their objects for attention.   

	Yet some of the show’s rather obtuse groupings (“Portraits,” “Animals,” “Bird in Space”) precluded more nuanced considerations, which might have included materials, questions of primitivism, gender, folk culture vs. high modernism, or any number of less literal taxonomies. One section bore the title “The Ambiguity of Form.” Perhaps no modernist artist proved less equivocal regarding form than Brancusi (save perhaps Mondrian). His sculptures evince a lapidary certainty even in their weird, seductive lyricisms.

	The elemental spareness of eggs and bones forms the metaphorical (and literal) touchstones of Brancusi’s series of resting heads (Sleep, Head of a Sleeping Child, The Newborn, etc.) and stylized “portraits” (Nancy Cunard, Eileen Lane, Princess X). The phallic arc of the latter sculpture—which caused a rumpus upon its debut at the 1920 Salon des Indépendants—exemplifies Brancusi’s conciliation of incongruous elements: lithe female corporeality and swollen male member; the mythical Leda and the Zeus-cum-swan who ravishes her; a young bird and the egg which birthed it.
	


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin. 
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	CHRISTIE’S PR VIGNETTE is not the first rendezvous between Brancusi’s legacy and something of the beau monde, as it were. A short film shot by Man Ray around 1930 on view herereveals Lee Miller running her hand over the smooth neck of Princess X. Rather than Miller’s budding career as a photographer, it is her fame as a model which seems the point here. The rhyme between her graceful form and the sculpture’s anatomy underscores the clip’s unmistakably erotic frisson.  

	Brancusi’s body of work has likewise informed the design of Balenciaga dresses, Rick Owens boots, and jewelry by the Tokyo-based Ambush firm—or, at least, it has informed their respective publicity campaigns. Among the objects that the Bulgari designer Mary Katrantzou wishes she had made, the T Magazine reported recently, figures Brancusi’s Sleeping Muse (1910) for its managing to be “devoid of any intricacy.” 

	Intricacy need not present itself as such, of course. In that paradox lies the beguiling complexity of Brancusi’s work, which he often carved frommarble, wood, or limestone without recourse to the molding process (what sculptors call taille directe). Even his cast bronze sculptures quite literally reflect the obsessive acts of polishing or the application of patina to which he submitted them. The modest volumes of Sleeping Muse, or Danaïde, or Bird in Space belie an intricate and iterative labor, which in turn erased its own traces. 
	

	Attesting to his labor is an ovoid pavilion at the exhibition’s center recreating Brancusi’s studio, chock-a-block with his myriad tools and flanked by walls on both sides bearing letters, photographs, and archival items. From postcard exchanges with Fernand Léger and Blaise Cendrars to documents of his artistic formation in Romania, the material puts intellectual, professional, and personal flesh back on the bareboned laconicism of his sculptures.

	The fundamentally subtractive ethos of Brancusi’s vision gave rise to a phenomenon that one journalist deemed—with a seemingly unironic oxymoron—a “minimalism glut” taking over contemporary American culture. Detailed by Kyle Chayka in his book The Longing for Less (2020), that sensibility informs everything from the penchant for sleek, streamlined appliances to “decluttered” lifestyle practices (at least, it must be said, among those with the means to dispense with luxury trappings or material excess to begin with).  


			
			
			
	
			
					View of the 2026 exhibition “Brancusi” at the Neue Nationalgalerie in Berlin. 
									Photo David von Becker. ©Succession Brancusi/VG Bild-Kunst
	



	Brancusi’s sensibility echoes elsewhere than high-end design or social trends, to be sure. The German curator Nicolaus Schafhausen explored the “The Brancusi Effect” on the work of several artists and architects in 2014. His exhibition and book notably featured the German architect Jürgen Mayer H. and industrial designer Konstantin Grcic; the sculptor and video artist Shahrayr Nashat; and a global group of conceptual artists including Sofia Hultén, André Cadere, and Saâdane Afif. The range in itself attests to the varied ramifications of Brancusi’s corpus. 
	

	Though it now sits behind glass at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, it was Brancusi’s marble Sculpture for the Blind (c. 1920) that shifted sculpture’s invitation to the viewer from the rational, metaphysical plane of sight to the embodied experience of touch. While not as frenziedly as Naum Gabo’s Kinetic Construction (Standing Wave) (1919–20), the buffed Leda (1926) was once mounted atop a spinning metal disc—footage of which appears in Berlin, along with a new rotating display.

	One wall text claims that Brancusi aimed to depict his animals in motion. Yet while Leda’s table may spin, her form remains singularly still. Seal reveals only the slightest of obliques, while the wooden Turtle (1940)—like The Cock (1924), Maiastra (1910), and other creatures—retain a hieraticism just shy of symmetry. The stateliness of Brancusi’s sculptures is never reducible to some platonic idea of nature, however. Even in the fixedness of their forms—their sententious certitude—a single work may conflate the erotic and the machinic, the vernacular and the archetypal, the abstract and the practical.

	First shipped stateside in 1926 for a retrospective organized by the photographer Edward Steichen, Bird in Space was initially charged with an import tax upon “manufactured metal objects.” Only a subsequent court case and deposition by the artist famously restored the work’s aesthetic pedigree on US soil, undoing its putative tax status as a “tool.” From Steichen (a keen photographer of the sculptor’s work) to Duchamp (a close confidant) to the collector John Quinn, Brancusi’s American reception inflects his oeuvre with a particular set of cultural, professional, and interpretive contingencies. What MoMA will make of these a hundred years later remains to be seen.

schema.headline: Why Brancusi’s Sleek, Streamlined Sculptures Still Seduce
